turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response: Hi. Well, I'm here because I just... I can't stop seeing this droop and unevenness around my mouth and jaw. Every time I look in a mirror or see a photo, it's right there, and it's all I can focus on. People keep telling me I look fine, but it just feels so obvious to me. It's gotten bad enough that I've actually started avoiding client meetings and presentations at work because I don't want anyone looking at my face.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived droop and unevenness around their mouth and jaw that others say looks fine, which is the core feature of body dysmorphic disorder.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself repeatedly checking mirrors, adjusting your face, or trying to hide the area throughout the day?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, all the time. Before work or any kind of family event, I can spend... well, hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I take pictures on my phone from different angles to see how the drooping looks, and I'm constantly redoing my makeup or adjusting my scarf to try and hide it. 

I also ask my husband over and over if my face looks lopsided. And then... I usually end up scrolling through photos of other women on my phone, just comparing myself to see how bad mine looks next to theirs. It takes up a lot of my time.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors such as checking mirrors for hours, taking photos from different angles, adjusting makeup and clothing to hide her face, seeking reassurance from her husband, and comparing herself to other women.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that your view of your face might be exaggerated, or are you completely certain that the defect is as severe as you see it?
turns.patient_response:
I know people tell me it's not that bad, or that I'm making a big deal out of nothing. But... I don't feel like I'm exaggerating at all. 

When I look in the mirror or see a picture, it's exactly as severe as I'm describing. The unevenness is just right there. So, yes, I'm certain it really looks that way, even if my husband or other people claim they don't notice it. I just don't understand how they can't see it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a perceived defect (unevenness in their face) that they are certain is severe, even though others claim they do not notice it.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this concern about your mouth and jaw?
turns.patient_response: I'm not really sure, to be honest. It feels like... well, it's been going on for a while now. I can't really give you a specific date or year when it started. It just sort of... became something I noticed, and then it got harder and harder to ignore. Now it's just an everyday thing.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that strangers or other people take special notice of your mouth, stare at it, or talk about it behind your back?
turns.patient_response: No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't really notice people staring at me on the street or anything like that. And I haven't heard anyone whispering about it behind my back. It's more just... my own awareness of it, I guess. I just know it's there, but I don't feel like strangers are pointing it out or focusing on it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies feeling that strangers stare at or talk about their mouth, ruling out referential delusions.
